answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Estragon says this at the opening of Beckett’s Waiting for Godot, while struggling with a boot. The publisher’s English excerpt confirms it; Beckett’s English version was published in 1954, separately from the 1952 French text.

source.heading: The source
trail: Grove’s primary excerpt ↗ identifies Estragon and the immediate boot-removal action.
The publication history ↗ distinguishes the English edition from the French text and stage premiere.
source.rightsHolder: Samuel Beckett’s estate / Grove Press and the relevant English publishers
source.rightsNote: The English wording belongs to Beckett’s 1954 self-translation of a modern play. This tiny excerpt is used to identify its speaker and dramatic context; it is not a public-domain work.

author.name: Samuel Beckett
author.heading: About Samuel Beckett
author.bio: Samuel Beckett wrote fiction and drama in both English and French, often translating and revising his own work between the two languages. His sparse settings and restless voices examine what remains when ordinary explanations and consolations stop working.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The first thing to defeat Estragon is a boot, before the play’s larger waiting has even begun. Vladimir takes the remark as a broader judgment and replies accordingly, allowing Beckett to move from a practical frustration to the pair’s enduring uncertainty without changing the words.

schema.claimReviewed: Samuel Beckett wrote Estragon’s opening line “Nothing to be done” in Waiting for Godot.
schema.faqAnswer: Yes. Estragon says it at the opening of Waiting for Godot in Beckett’s own English version, first published in 1954.
schema.verdictNote: Beckett wrote the line; Estragon is its fictional speaker.
